title: Frege’s Theorem and Foundations for Arithmetic

summaries.example: Imagine two groups: three apples and three toy cars. Even though the things are different, you can pair each apple with one car, with nothing left over. Frege calls this a one-to-one matching. Hume’s Principle says that groups with such a matching have the same number. Frege then uses ideas about matching and “the next number” to show why zero, successors, and counting rules can be proved in a logical system.
summaries.summary: Frege’s Theorem is a result about the foundations of arithmetic. Frege tried to show that basic facts about natural numbers could come from logic. His key idea was Hume’s Principle: two concepts have the same number when their objects can be paired one-to-one. With second-order logic, this principle supports proofs about zero, the next number, induction, and the natural numbers. Frege’s original system also included Basic Law V, a rule about extensions, or something like collections of objects. That rule led to Russell’s Paradox and made the full system inconsistent. However, the proofs of the basic arithmetic rules do not essentially use Basic Law V after Hume’s Principle is taken as a starting point. This leaves important questions about how numbers exist and how we know which objects they are.
key_ideas: Frege wanted to explain arithmetic using logic rather than relying on pictures, experiments, or special intuition.
To compare numbers, Frege compared groups by one-to-one matching.
Hume’s Principle connects matching groups with equality of their numbers.
Using second-order logic, Frege’s work derives rules about zero, successors, induction, and the natural numbers.
A different rule, Basic Law V, made Frege’s original larger system inconsistent because it led to Russell’s Paradox.
The successful proof can be separated from Basic Law V, so the arithmetic result does not need that troublesome rule.
summaries.why_it_matters: Arithmetic seems familiar, but philosophers ask why its rules are true and what numbers really are. Frege’s work gives a detailed attempt to build arithmetic from logic and matching. It also teaches an important lesson about theories: a theory may contain a serious error while still containing a valuable idea that can be separated and studied on its own. The remaining questions about the existence and identity of numbers continue to matter for the philosophy of mathematics.

important_terms.definition: A careful system for deciding whether statements fit together and for drawing conclusions from them.
A number that answers “How many?” for a group of things.
A matching in which every item in one group is paired with exactly one item in another group, and vice versa.
The rule that two concepts have the same number exactly when their objects can be matched one-to-one.
The idea that number rules can be proved from Hume’s Principle using second-order logic.
A problem in Frege’s larger system where a rule about collections leads to a contradiction.

questions_to_think_about: Why does a one-to-one matching show that two groups have the same number?
Is proving arithmetic from logic the same as explaining what numbers are?
Why might a rule that seems helpful accidentally create a contradiction?
What would a good definition of number need to tell us about unusual objects?

summaries.example: Let F be the concept “is a student in a particular three-person debate team” and G the concept “is a day in a three-day school trip.” If there is a relation that pairs each F-object with exactly one G-object, and each G-object with exactly one F-object, then F and G are equinumerous. Hume’s Principle represents this by saying that the number of Fs equals the number of Gs exactly when F and G are equinumerous. Frege’s construction then defines zero from a concept with no instances, defines natural numbers through the predecessor relation, and uses its ancestral and weak ancestral to obtain the Peano-style principles.
summaries.summary: The entry reconstructs Frege’s attempt to ground arithmetic in logic. In a modern second-order predicate calculus, variables range not only over objects but also over concepts and relations. Frege’s central numerical idea is equinumerosity: concepts are equinumerous when a one-to-one relation connects their instances. Hume’s Principle states that the number belonging to one concept is identical to the number belonging to another exactly when the concepts are equinumerous. From this principle, the entry develops definitions of predecessor, the ancestral of a relation, and the weak ancestral. Natural numbers are characterized as the members of the predecessor-series beginning with zero. The proof then derives the Dedekind/Peano axioms: zero is a natural number, zero has no natural predecessor, successors are unique, induction holds, and every natural number has a successor. Frege’s original system also used Basic Law V to govern extensions. Together with comprehension, it yields Russell’s Paradox and inconsistency. The arithmetic derivation can nevertheless be isolated from that failed part. Philosophical difficulties remain: Hume’s Principle does not by itself settle which arbitrary objects are numbers, and its status as a purely logical principle is debated in the entry’s discussion.
key_ideas: Frege analyzes a number statement as concerning a concept: asking “how many?” requires specifying what kind of things are being counted.
Equinumerosity is defined by the existence of a relation establishing a one-to-one correspondence between the objects falling under two concepts.
Hume’s Principle is a contextual definition of numerical identity, not an explicit account of which arbitrary objects are numbers.
Frege defines zero using the number of a concept with no instances, and natural numbers as members of the predecessor-series beginning with zero.
The resulting derivation establishes zero’s status, non-repetition of successors, mathematical induction, and the existence of a successor for every natural number.

Basic Law V, which identifies extensions when concepts have the same instances, produces inconsistency through Russell’s Paradox; its failure does not infect the later derivation from Hume’s Principle alone.
summaries.why_it_matters: Frege’s Theorem is important because it shows how much arithmetic can be obtained from a single principle about one-to-one correspondence, together with second-order logic. It separates a powerful mathematical achievement from the inconsistency of Frege’s broader theory of extensions. The entry also exposes a difference between deriving arithmetic laws and justifying the existence and identity of numbers. That difference is central to logicism and to continuing debates about the foundations of mathematics.

important_terms.definition: A formal language whose variables can range over objects and also over properties or relations; this permits quantification over concepts.
A property or condition under which objects fall; in the modern reconstruction, one-place relations are treated as concepts.
The relation holding between two concepts when a relation pairs their instances one-to-one.
A principle stating that the numbers of two concepts are identical if and only if the concepts are equinumerous.
A relation that links an item to later items in a chain, rather than only to its immediate successor.
A relation that includes both the ancestral links and identity, useful for describing a series beginning with a first item.
Frege’s result that Dedekind/Peano axioms follow from Hume’s Principle in second-order logic.

questions_to_think_about: Does equinumerosity explain what numbers are, or only when two numbers are equal?
Why is a relation such as “immediately precedes” insufficient by itself to define an entire numerical series?
How does induction differ from merely listing 0, 1, 2, and so on?
Can Hume’s Principle be accepted as a logical truth if it implies the existence of numbers?
What does the Julius Caesar problem show about defining numbers by identity conditions alone?

summaries.example: Suppose a club has four members and a game has four playing pieces. You can show the groups have the same size by pairing each member with one piece, with no member or piece left unmatched. The members and pieces do not need to be the same kind of thing. Frege’s idea is that numbers depend on this structure of matching. Later, imagine a number line where each number has a next number. Frege builds this “next” relation from the idea of removing one object from a group, then uses chains of such relations to describe all the natural numbers starting at zero.
summaries.summary: Frege’s Theorem concerns an ambitious question: can the basic truths of arithmetic be derived from logic? Frege begins with concepts, which classify objects, and with equinumerosity, the relation between concepts whose instances can be matched one-to-one. Hume’s Principle says that two concepts have the same number exactly when they are equinumerous. Using second-order logic, Frege defines zero, the immediate-predecessor relation, and broader relations that trace a whole series. Natural numbers are then the objects in the predecessor-series beginning with zero. From these resources, he derives the main Dedekind/Peano principles, including induction and the claim that every natural number has a successor. Frege’s original project also included Basic Law V, intended to explain extensions, roughly like collections determined by concepts. With comprehension, this principle generates Russell’s Paradox, so the full system is inconsistent. The important result is that the arithmetic derivation can be separated from that problematic principle. The entry ends by examining whether Hume’s Principle adequately explains the existence and identity of numbers.
key_ideas: Frege’s goal was to explain arithmetic through logic, a project often called logicism.
A number is connected to a concept: “the number of F-things” depends on which objects fall under F.
Equinumerosity captures sameness of number without requiring the matched objects to be alike.
Hume’s Principle supplies the main bridge from one-to-one matching to numerical identity.
Frege uses predecessor and longer chains, called ancestrals, to define the natural-number series rather than simply writing an endless list.
The derivation of the basic arithmetic principles can use Hume’s Principle without relying essentially on Basic Law V, the source of the contradiction in the larger system.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theorem matters both mathematically and philosophically. Mathematically, it shows that familiar arithmetic structure can emerge from a principle about matching and a powerful logical framework. Philosophically, it distinguishes two questions that are easy to confuse: how to derive the laws governing numbers, and why numbers exist or which objects they are. Frege’s failure with Basic Law V also illustrates why foundational theories must be checked for consistency, not just judged by how elegant their definitions appear.

important_terms.definition: A method of reasoning in which rules determine which conclusions follow from given statements.
A description or property used to sort objects, such as “is a club member” or “is even.”
Having the same number of instances because the instances can be paired one-to-one.
The claim that two concepts have the same number exactly when their instances can be put into a one-to-one correspondence.
A rule or statement accepted as a starting point in a theory.
A system that allows a contradiction, meaning a statement and its negation can both be derived.
A contradiction produced by considering a collection of all collections that do not contain themselves.
A proof rule saying that if a property starts with zero and continues from each number to its next number, it holds for every natural number.

questions_to_think_about: Why can two groups contain different kinds of objects but still have the same number?
Why is a list of numerals not enough to prove that every natural number has a successor?
What does mathematical induction add to ordinary step-by-step counting?
Should Hume’s Principle count as a definition, an axiom, or a logical truth?
How can a theory contain a useful proof even after another part of the same theory is shown to be inconsistent?
